newsitem.title: FRANCE: French probe into Scientology led up blind alleys.
newsitem.headline: French probe into Scientology led up blind alleys.

text.p: Police probing the French Church of Scientology told a court on Thursday their attempts to study its finances led mostly up blind alleys as church officials around the world claimed ignorance when questioned.
"The church was highly structured, but no one could answer our questions, whether we went to Copenhagen, Denmark or Luxembourg," police investigator Alain Helfrich said.
"The people we encountered did not appear wealthy, but I am convinced that this money went overseas to unknown individuals, probably in the United States," he said.

Helfrich was testifying on the fourth day of a trial of 23 current and former church followers in the central French city of Lyon on charges ranging from manslaughter to embezzlement to fraud and complicity.
If found guilty, the defendants face up to five years in jail and fines of up to five million francs ($1 million).
The trial was prompted by the 1988 suicide of a church follower in Lyon and a later crackdown on cults by the French government.
Widow Nelly Vic charged after the death of her husband Patrice that the church had driven him to suicide by pressuring him to take costly church courses for which he lacked the money.
The religion, founded in 1954 by the late American science-fiction novelist L. Ron Hubbard, claims more than eight million adherents worldwide, including 4,000 in France.

Prosecutors accuse the church of "exploiting the good faith and gullibility of its victims for commercial profit, through pseudo-scientific and paramedical means, to their financial detriment and at their medical and psychological risk".
Church of Scientology spokesman Marc Bromberg has denounced the proceeding as "heresy".
Helfrich and colleage Etienne Mozul said they were eventually able to identify several church accounts in France including one set up in Paris by a church arm in Copenhagen.
They said 16 million francs ($3.1 million) had been withdrawn from the account between 1988 and 1991 for unknown destinations.

Two other accounts in Luxembourg and Britain were used to pool money collected from church followers in Europe and funnel it Clearwater, Florida, in the United States, where it was used to finance the training of high-level church officials. in Clearwater, Florida, in the United States.
The trial is expected to conclude after three more days of testimony.
